```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = TRUE)
```

We will use StatgenGWAS to perform a GWAS

## Load libraries

```{r, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(statgenGWAS) #needed for GWAS
library(here)
```

## Load data

```{r}
snp_dir <- "/analyzed_data/GWAS_workshop/data/filtered_snps"
```

### SNP data

```{r}
geno <- readPLINK(
  bed = file.path(snp_dir, "WL2_2025_merge_filtered.bed")
)
# will also read the .bim and .fam files

# edit names to match format in phenotype data
rownames(geno$markers) <- str_remove(rownames(geno$markers), "WL2_.*_.*_")

# impute missing marker data and clean up the snp matrix
# this probably should be run with the beagle method, but for time consideration, using the "random" method
# this is memory intensive.

# 2 minutes
system.time(geno <-  codeMarkers(geno) )

str(geno)
```

### Kinship and PCs

Kinship
```{r}
kinship_names <- read_tsv(file.path(snp_dir, "WL2_2025_merge_filtered_kinship.rel.id"),
    col_names = c("rownames", "colnames")) %>% 
  mutate(across(everything(),  \(x) str_remove(x, "WL2_.*_.*_")) # match phenotype naming format
)

all(kinship_names$rownames == kinship_names$colnames) # TRUE

kinship_matrix <- read_table(
    file.path(snp_dir, "WL2_2025_merge_filtered_kinship.rel"),
    col_names = FALSE) %>% 
    as.matrix()

dimnames(kinship_matrix) <- list(kinship_names$rownames, kinship_names$colnames)

kinship_matrix[1:5, 1:5]
```

PCs
```{r}
PCs_pct_var <- read_table(
        file.path(snp_dir, "WL2_2025_merge_filtered_pca.eigenval"),
        col_names = "Pct_Var") %>% 
      mutate(PC= str_c("PC", 1:n()))
 
 PCs_pct_var
```

```{r}
PCs <- read_table(
        file = file.path(snp_dir, "WL2_2025_merge_filtered_pca.eigenvec"),
        col_names = c("Unique.ID", "ID1", PCs_pct_var$PC))  %>%
      select(-ID1) %>% # remove duplicate column of names
      mutate(Unique.ID = str_remove(Unique.ID, "WL2_.*_.*_")) # match phenotype format
 
    head(PCs)
```

### phenotypes

```{r}
size <- read_csv(here("GWAS-traditional", "data", "WL2_2025_Size-Merged.csv"))
head(size)

# pick a single date to work on, for now
size_2025_06_09 <- size %>% 
  filter(survey_date == "2025-06-09", Unique.ID %in% rownames(geno$markers)) %>%
  arrange(match(Unique.ID, rownames(geno$markers))) # ensure order matches genotype.
                                                    # Not sure that this matters but can't hurt...

head(size_2025_06_09)
```

### Phenotype & PCA plots

Let's explore how the phenotype is distributed among the PC axes

```{r}
PC_size <- inner_join(size_2025_06_09, PCs, by = "Unique.ID")
dim(PC_size)
head(PC_size)
```

First a histogram of our trait.
```{r}
PC_size %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = height.cm)) +
  geom_histogram()
```
skewed.  log transform?

```{r}
PC_size %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = height.cm)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  scale_x_log10()
```
much better

```{r}
PC_size %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=PC1, y=PC2, color = log2(height.cm))) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_color_viridis_c()
```
Some structure associated with trait.

## GWAS

We need to bring the genetic and phenotypic data together into one gData object for statgen

```{r}
# need slight modification to the pheno tibble before combining
size_2025_06_09_pheno <- size_2025_06_09 %>% 
  select(genotype = Unique.ID, height.cm, overhd.diam, overhd.perp, herbv.scale, leaf.number) %>%
  mutate(l2.height.cm = log2(height.cm))

# confirm order
all(size_2025_06_09_pheno$genotype == rownames(geno$markers))

# also will use bed and PCs as possible covariate, create a dataframe for this
# here, confusingly, the genotype IDs are in the rownames

covar <- PC_size %>%
  select(Unique.ID, bed, PC1:PC10) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  column_to_rownames("Unique.ID")

all(rownames(covar)== rownames(geno$markers))


geno_pheno <- createGData(gData = geno,
                          kin = kinship_matrix,
                          pheno = size_2025_06_09_pheno,
                          covar = covar)
                          


str(geno_pheno)
```

### Run the GWAS
We will compare GWAS run with a few different population structure corrections and methods.  Also will try including bed as a covariate to correct for bed-to-bed variation

1. No correction
2. Population PCs as covariate
3. Kinship matrix as correction
4. PCs and Kinship as correction
5. PCs and Kinship as correction + bed

Run the code below, replacing TRAIT with the name of your trait.

#### No correction

To see what the GWAS looks like with no correction we will give statgenGWAS a matrix filled with zeros.

```{r}
#define our zero matrix
nullmat <- matrix(0, ncol=ncol(kinship_matrix),nrow=nrow(kinship_matrix), dimnames = dimnames(kinship_matrix))

# run the GWAS
## 2.5 minutes
system.time(gwas.noCorrection <- runSingleTraitGwas(gData = geno_pheno,
                                       traits = "l2.height.cm",
                                       kin = nullmat)
)
```

We can get a quick summary with:
```{r}
summary(gwas.noCorrection)
```


We can look at the Q-Q plot with:
```{r}
plot(gwas.noCorrection, plotType = "qq")
```
And a Manhattan plot with:
```{r}
plot(gwas.noCorrection, plotType = "manhattan")
```
In the Manhattan plot, each dot is a SNP.  SNPs in red are above the significance threshold. If you see a lot of red, then that means that many, many SNPs were significant.

### PCA as population correction

Let's see if things improve if we correct for population structure.  One methods is to include the PCs as co-variates in the analysis.  You can this with:

```{r}
# run the GWAS
system.time(
gwas.PCA <- runSingleTraitGwas(gData = geno_pheno,
                               traits = "l2.height.cm",
                               kin = nullmat,
                               covar = c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3", "PC4", "PC5")
            )
)
```

Again, you can summarize and plot with:
```{r}
summary(gwas.PCA)

plot(gwas.PCA, plotType = "qq")

plot(gwas.PCA, plotType = "manhattan")
```

### Kinship Matrix

An alternative strategy for population structure correction is to use a kinship matrix, which provides the genetic relatedness of each plant to all of the others.

```{r}
# run the GWAS
system.time(
gwas.K <- runSingleTraitGwas(gData = geno_pheno,
                             traits = "l2.height.cm")
                             # since we have a kinship matrix in gData that will be used
)
```

```{r}
summary(gwas.K)

plot(gwas.K, plotType = "qq", ggtitle = "Height--Kinship Correction")

plot(gwas.K, plotType = "manhattan", ggtitle = "Height--Kinship Correction")
```

### Kinship Matrix + PCA

```{r}
# run the GWAS
system.time(
  gwas.K.pca <- runSingleTraitGwas(gData = geno_pheno,
                             traits = "l2.height.cm",
                             covar = c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3", "PC4", "PC5")
  )
)
```

```{r}
summary(gwas.K.pca)

plot(gwas.K.pca, plotType = "qq", ggtitle = "Height--Kinship + PCA Correction")

plot(gwas.K.pca, plotType = "manhattan", ggtitle = "Height--Kinship + PCA Correction")
```

### Kinship Matrix + PCA + bed
```{r}
# run the GWAS
system.time(
  gwas.K.pca.bed <- runSingleTraitGwas(gData = geno_pheno,
                             traits = "l2.height.cm",
                             covar = c("bed", "PC1", "PC2", "PC3", "PC4", "PC5")
  )
)
```

```{r}
summary(gwas.K.pca.bed)

plot(gwas.K.pca.bed, plotType = "qq", ggtitle = "Height--Kinship + PCA Correction")

plot(gwas.K.pca.bed, plotType = "manhattan", ggtitle = "Height--Kinship + PCA Correction"))
```


## get the significant SNPs

```{r, eval=FALSE}
sigSnps <- gwas.PCA$signSnp[[1]]
sigSnps
```
In this table, some of the column names should be obvious. Here are some of the others:

* allFreq: the minor allele frequency at that SNP
* effect: the change in the trait value associated with the SNP
* effectSE: the standard error of the estimated effect
* RLR2: likelihood-ratio-based R<sup>2</sup> as defined in Sun et al. (2010)
* LOD: -log10(P) (which isn't a true LOD score...)
* propSnpVar: of the total variance in the trait, what proportion is "explained" by this SNP
